assertions.rationale: The supplied eight-page text describes input monitoring and possible use of clinical information, but does not specify measurement-level source identity, units, acquisition/availability times, transformations or dataset versions. Proposed auditability of decisions is not variable-level data provenance. No operational provenance feature is established; this does not demonstrate its absence from an unspecified future implementation.

No retention or reversible representation of actual clinical event/acquisition timestamps is described. References to real-time trust monitoring and changing regulations concern proposed operational governance, not preservation of observation timestamps. Mentioning a patient-history LLM module does not establish its temporal input contract.

The proposed healthcare workflow does not distinguish information-release time from collection time or define when notes, diagnostic results or historical information become usable. No training/query construction protocol establishes availability-aware inputs. Neither leakage nor correct availability handling can be inferred.

Section III proposes screening queries for incomplete context, but does not specify measured/missing/invalid indicators supplied to any model. Listing 1 scores responses rather than defining a clinical observation tensor or missingness treatment. Incomplete-context screening alone does not establish availability masks.

No per-variable time-since-observation representation, carry-forward mechanism or freshness update is specified for clinical information. Continuous monitoring of trust is not measurement-age tracking. The paper does not document enough of the proposed patient-history processing to resolve this feature.

No prediction mechanism consumes actual unequal observation intervals, native events or continuous clinical time. The described adaptation and ethical-refinement loop concern governance, not irregular-time prediction. The source also does not establish an incompatible uniform-spacing implementation, so absence is not asserted.

Input monitoring and clinician referral are proposed response-governance operations. The paper does not model when, whether or why clinical measurements occur conditional on patient state or acquisition context. No implemented observation-generation rule or corresponding evaluation is reported.

The supplied text reports no target-specific resampling study, sampling grid or comparison of witnesses in values, cell-level updates, native timing and external channels. General auditability and monitoring discussions do not constitute an observation-clock audit. No completed incompatible preprocessing review establishes explicit absence.

Sector-specific trust weighting and task-specialized LLM routing are described, but no source-to-target mapping of clinical units, terminology or measurement definitions is specified. Domain customization is not evidence of semantic data harmonization. No mapping implementation or conversion validation is reported.

No development/evaluation dataset, patient/site/time partition, preprocessing-fit protocol or feature-availability audit is reported for this framework. The conceptual application descriptions cannot establish leakage control, but their lack of an empirical protocol also does not prove leakage occurred.

The proposed framework does not specify participating data sites, local record retention or a federated training/query protocol with exchanged artifacts. References [1] and [14] concern federated systems, but bibliography entries do not establish federation in this contribution. Privacy and regulatory motivation likewise do not establish this mechanism.

Figures describe specialized LLM modules and the pseudocode assumes an existing response object, but neither specifies an operational observation-to-state/features encoder. No named architecture, input representation or executed encoder path is reported. Ordinary internal capabilities of unspecified LLMs are not inherited as evidence for this feature.

No named pretrained checkpoint/version, encoder parameters, transferred features or adaptation procedure is identified. Generic LLM boxes and specialization labels do not establish foundation-encoder reuse. The source also does not state that an encoder was trained from scratch, so an absent assessment is unwarranted.

Listing 1 specifies an illustrative weighted response-trust score, not a loss predicting target representations from context. No representation-training objective or execution is reported for the framework or its unspecified LLM modules. Trust-score aggregation is not treated as latent prediction, and unspecified base-model objectives are not inferred.

No predictive representation-training specification, anti-collapse constraint, target-network mechanism or representation-collapse result is reported. Bias checks and inter-model consistency checks concern response governance rather than representation collapse. Because the underlying training mechanisms are unspecified, neither absence nor dependency-based inapplicability is established.

The paper discusses generating or summarizing language responses but supplies no loss comparing reconstructed observations with reference observations. Listing 1 is a response-scoring illustration, not an observation-reconstruction training objective. The source neither specifies reconstruction training nor explicitly excludes it from the unnamed underlying models.

The proposed healthcare workflow combines outputs from LLM modules specializing in guidelines, diagnostic data and patient history. These specializations do not identify two distinct input modalities with a specified, executed multimodal fusion operation. Model-output aggregation alone does not establish this feature.

Input screening for incomplete context is discussed, but no fusion mechanism uses observed modality availability, quality or recency, and no missing-modality behavior is defined. The proposed trust layer does not establish availability-aware multimodal fusion.

The framework specifies response processing and an illustrative trust-scoring function, but defines no explicit or latent health-world state or event history carried into subsequent prediction/update steps. Continuous monitoring terminology does not establish persistent evolving state. No implemented state mechanism is reported.

Listing 1 invokes response variance as a trust-score component. It does not define hidden-state variables, a history-conditioned posterior or a filtering distribution. Background references to Bayesian methods cannot establish a belief-state mechanism in this proposed framework.

No prior health-state evolution or observation-conditioned correction operation is specified. The ethical-governance refinement loop concerns oversight rather than filtering, and does not describe treatment of missing observations. This reporting gap does not establish an implemented incompatible assimilation algorithm.

Patient history is named as an LLM specialization, but the paper does not describe updating an individual's current state from newly arriving clinical observations during sequential use. Adaptive monitoring and stakeholder-feedback cycles do not establish patient-state assimilation.

Sector-specific score weighting and future adaptation to changing regulations concern governance configuration. No patient-specific parameters, model-weight updates, measurement-driven fitting rule or corresponding execution is reported. A patient-history module does not establish individual parameter adaptation.

The paper discusses several sectors and healthcare applications, but identifies no shared state representation or checkpoint feeding at least two typed tasks. Reuse of a conceptual governance architecture is not reuse of a learned patient state.

The narrative applications and simplified scoring example report no state/history ablations or probes against a defined prediction or decision target. The recommendation to develop trust-oriented benchmarks is future work, not a state-sufficiency assessment. No explicit negative assessment statement is reported.

The healthcare illustration names a patient-history-specialized LLM, but does not specify how prior observations/actions condition an inferred state or forecast. No history encoding, temporal input semantics or executed history-conditioning mechanism is reported. The module label alone does not meet the feature criteria.

No matched history-swap, withholding, population-prior or analogous individual-information control is reported. Naming patient history in a proposed triage workflow and claiming tangible case-study value do not demonstrate patient-specific predictive value.

Consistency in the trust framework concerns agreement or consistency of LLM responses. No memory, loss or constraint preserves patient identity, anatomy or modeled entities through health-world transitions. The warning that models can agree incorrectly is a conceptual limitation, not a tested identity-consistency mechanism or observed identity failure.

Explainability and interpretable rationales are proposed trust priorities, and added opacity is acknowledged. The paper supplies no state variables with a documented mapping to clinical entities or physiology and no state-inspection functionality. A proposed explanation of a response is not inspectable state semantics.

No recurrent memory, attention-context specification, retrieval store or other mechanism retains prior patient observations/actions beyond a current supplied state. Patient-history specialization and continuous governance do not identify an operational temporal-memory mechanism or its context length.

Delivering, flagging or referring an LLM response are proposed governance decisions. They are not specified as settable action inputs conditioning predictions of clinical or other world-state consequences. The domain argument in the illustrative scoring function selects policy context, not a clinical intervention. No qualifying action-input mechanism is reported.

The paper distinguishes application sectors, LLM specializations and governance outcomes, but does not define action roles with physiological, observational, procedural or system effect channels. Diagnostic triage, summarization and patient communication are discussed as tasks, not an operational typed action vocabulary. No qualifying role/channel implementation is established.

The healthcare illustration describes symptom queries, specialized LLM responses and clinician referral. It does not define a settable clinical intervention or command with applicable parameters, units, timing, duration or reference-frame semantics. The referral description alone does not establish a parameterized world-model action interface.

No intervention start/stop times, action-sequence cadence or duration/dose schedule is reported. The order of processing layers and the proposed governance-refinement loop describe workflow, not a time-indexed intervention schedule. Their presence does not establish scheduling capability.

The paper combines response-scoring dimensions and discusses specialized LLM modules, but reports no joint treatment representation, co-intervention dependencies or replacement/inheritance semantics for unchanged settings. Weighted aggregation of trust signals is not evidence of a coherent treatment bundle.

Compliance scoring and low-trust referral are proposed, but context-dependent clinical action bounds, contraindications or workspace restrictions are not specified or tested. The unspecified trust threshold governs response delivery; it does not establish a constraint mechanism over candidate therapeutic or physical actions.

The workflow names response delivery and referral to a clinician, but does not define model action variables and their operational mapping to clinical procedures, calibrated device commands or executable interventions. No latent-action grounding procedure or operational integration result is reported. Naming a referral destination does not establish executable action grounding.

No historical action dataset, context-conditioned overlap estimate, coverage criterion or mechanistic support test for queried alternatives is reported. Response consistency, policy alignment and uncertainty-triggered referral are different mechanisms and do not establish support for intervention regimes.

Neither the narrative healthcare application nor the claimed case-study benefits report predicted successors under two specified actions from the same initial patient, scene or history. Comparing multiple LLM responses or describing delivery versus referral is not a matched alternative-action prediction experiment. Functional L3 evidence is therefore not established.

The paper discusses patient safety, misleading advice and escalation, but reports no assessment of action reversibility or residual harm after a response or recommendation has affected care. This remains relevant to the proposed high-stakes information workflow; conceptual status and lack of demonstrated actuation do not make harm reversibility automatically inapplicable.

The proposed pipeline scores responses and governs their delivery. No carried health-world state/history is mapped to a subsequent state or observation under a declared temporal or successor coordinate. Continuous monitoring and governance refinement are discussed, but no transition rule is reported; workflow arrows are not clinical-state dynamics.

No transition-learning objective, fitted physiological transition parameters, learned closure or hybrid state-evolution mechanism is reported. The explicitly simplified trust-scoring pseudocode does not document learned health-world dynamics. LLM use and the abstract's monitoring-implementation claim cannot establish an implemented learned transition.

The healthcare example conditions response generation on a symptom query and discusses routing by trust score. It does not report a transition consuming a settable intervention/regime or future-state results conditioned on that intervention. Query dependence and governance decisions do not establish action-conditioned patient dynamics or causal effects.

The paper discusses probabilistic LLM outputs and includes a response-variance term in illustrative pseudocode. It does not specify or execute a non-degenerate next-state distribution conditional on health-world state and action. Response variability cannot be reassigned to a stochastic transition, and no deterministic transition is sufficiently specified to justify an absent assessment.

No physiological equations, conservation laws, anatomy constraints, monotonicity rules, object structure or symbolic mechanism is reported as constraining representation or transition learning/inference. Clinical-guideline specialization, compliance scoring and named regulations do not themselves establish such an inductive bias.

The proposed composition combines LLM response generation, trust scoring and governance, but does not identify a mechanistic dynamics component operationally coupled to a learned component. Fixed, fitted and learned health-world quantities are not distinguished. Combining software layers or human oversight with LLMs is not evidence of mechanistic–learned hybrid dynamics.

Several specialized LLMs are envisioned, but no two dynamics implementations are exchanged under a documented common state/action/time/output contract. Model identities, semantic compatibility and integration or replacement tests are not reported. Multi-LLM orchestration alone does not establish interchangeable world-model backends.

The paper discusses multiple industries, specialized response modules and governance layers, but reports no physical, spatial or temporal health-world levels exchanging state or constraints through explicit cross-scale mappings. Sector-specific trust weighting and an iterative oversight cycle do not establish coupled multiscale dynamics.

The supplied full text describes a response-governance pipeline and illustrative score aggregation, but reports no dynamics-training objective traversing predicted states across two or more world transitions. Neither gradient propagation nor teacher-forcing behavior is specified. The pseudocode weights are aggregation parameters, not a reported multi-step learning loss.

The architecture has processing layers and an ethical-governance feedback cycle. The paper does not specify variable-duration options, event-level world transitions, subgoals, or coordinated higher/lower temporal resolutions. Architectural layering and iterative governance do not establish temporal abstraction.

LLM responses are proposed outputs for trust assessment, but no emission mapping from a declared internal health-world state to observable quantities is reported. An unspecified language model's ability to produce text does not establish an observation decoder for a world-transition model. Its internal architecture is not supplied.

The listing aggregates response-level trust signals, while the healthcare narrative names triage, summarization and communication. No defined heads map maintained states or trajectories to named clinical outcomes with targets, units and horizons. Trust-score components and task labels alone do not meet this feature's readout criteria.

The narrative applications and conclusion do not report an experiment predicting a later clinical state or justified transition successor against a reference. No future target, evaluation split, prediction metric or result is supplied. Claims of demonstrated case-study value cannot substitute for future-state prediction results.

No protocol advances generated world state or history through at least two successive transitions. The sequence of processing modules and the governance-refinement loop do not document free-running future simulation. The abstract's monitoring-implementation claim does not establish such a rollout.

The paper reports no evaluated successor sequence with ground-truth intermediate states or observations supplied between prediction steps. Mentioning patient history as an LLM specialization does not specify teacher-forced evaluation. The missing sequence-evaluation protocol does not establish either teacher forcing or its absence.

Clinician referral, patient-history specialization and stakeholder feedback are described, but no newly measured clinical observation corrects a propagated state before another forecast or plan. Governance feedback is not evidence of real-observation re-assimilation.

No furthest tested prediction extent, transition count or clinical-time cadence is reported. Continuous monitoring and future scalability are discussed without a forecast-horizon experiment. Operational query volume or governance iterations would not establish a maximum evaluated world-prediction horizon.

The monitoring discussion does not supply free-running prediction errors or validity violations at multiple forecast depths under a common protocol. Monitoring response reliability under contextual or distribution shifts is distinct from measuring compounding rollout error. No drift-test result is established.

No usable prediction horizon is supported by an error, calibration or decision curve with an explicit tolerance, uncertainty and action-support context. The unspecified trust threshold for clinician referral is not a temporal validity limit and does not establish a validated forecasting horizon.

Multiple LLM responses and an unspecified response-variance function are discussed, but no conditional future trajectories or explicit joint forecast distribution are reported. Neither parallel response generation nor agreement between models establishes temporal dependence across sampled world futures.

The framework proposes approving, flagging or escalating responses based on trust. It does not report a policy that checks requested prediction horizons against supported limits and rejects, transparently truncates or escalates out-of-horizon queries. Generic uncertainty-based escalation does not establish horizon enforcement.

Trust signals are proposed to govern delivery or referral of current responses. The paper does not report simulated future states or outcomes feeding action ranking, search, value learning or a future-grounded decision pathway. Response arbitration is not sufficient evidence of world-model use for decisions.

No operational optimizer or learned policy using modeled consequences or imagined trajectories is reported, nor are decision/control results supplied. The fixed-weight scoring example and proposed governance routing do not establish world-model-coupled optimization or L4 capability.

The paper does not specify executing a plan prefix, acquiring new real observations and recomputing a plan, with planning and execution horizons. The ethical-governance cycle and clinician handoff do not establish receding-horizon replanning. No execution or replanning evaluation is reported.

assertions.applicability_reason: The assessed contribution specifies response scoring and governance, not a learned world-state transition coupled to a utility optimizer. There is therefore no transition whose reuse under changed planning objectives can be assessed. Domain-specific trust weights are not objective-independent dynamics.
assertions.rationale: This assessment concerns the proposed architecture, not an inferred absence of objective separation in the unspecified LLMs.

The healthcare workflow specifies clinician referral when the resulting trust score falls below a threshold, making uncertainty relevant to response acceptance.
assertions.rationale: The feature's decision-selection criterion is met at specification stage for response delivery versus referral. No execution, threshold validation, calibrated uncertainty, world-model planner or L4 capability is established.

assertions.applicability_reason: The proposed framework does not optimize plans within predictive world dynamics. Consequently, testing whether such optimized plans exploit transition-model error is outside this contribution's defined mechanism.
assertions.rationale: Adversarial input screening and the warning about shared LLM errors concern other assurance questions; they do not instantiate a planner-exploitation experiment.

assertions.applicability_reason: The architecture routes queries to specialized LLMs and arbitrates their responses; it does not construct candidate action regimes for world-model planning. Identifying generic response-producing modules does not supply a candidate-action set to which this feature's eligibility, support and coverage requirements apply.
assertions.rationale: The provenance and coverage of the generated responses remain underspecified, but that reporting limitation is not recoded as provenance of simulated clinical actions.

assertions.applicability_reason: The described layers perform input screening, response orchestration, scoring and governance. They do not constitute a model-coupled action policy with higher-level goals/options and lower-level actions governed by durations or termination conditions.
assertions.rationale: Architectural layering and clinician referral are not a temporal decision-policy hierarchy.

assertions.applicability_reason: The assessed specification concerns response governance, not a controller acting on an environment and using subsequent environmental observations for further control decisions. The ethical-governance refinement loop is not a closed-loop control protocol.
assertions.rationale: No clinical-time control loop is inferred from stakeholder feedback, monitoring aspirations or referral arrows.

Listing 1 invokes response.variance() but does not define the random variable, sampling procedure, predicted target, distribution, uncertainty set or component scale. Across the supplied eight-page text, these semantics are not supplied for this framework. The numerical proxy supports the specified use of uncertainty in routing, but does not sufficiently specify predictive uncertainty under this feature's criteria. Background Bayesian and dropout methods are not assigned to the proposal.

The supplied full text does not define separate aleatoric and epistemic components, their estimation procedures or their limitations for the proposed trust engine. The simplified single variance term does not establish a decomposition, but is not treated as a complete implemented uncertainty mechanism proving that decomposition is absent.

Although the healthcare narrative prioritizes uncertainty calibration, the paper reports no calibration sample, target frequency or coverage, reliability metric, reference outcomes or calibration result for this framework. A trust-score threshold and variance-based pseudocode are not a calibration evaluation.

assertions.applicability_reason: The defined product is an arbitrated response or clinician referral, not a multi-time predicted trajectory with a rollout/action regime. Therefore joint-path or horizon-indexed trajectory calibration has no specified target in this architecture.
assertions.rationale: Changing trust over governance cycles does not create a clinical trajectory forecast. Calibration of the response-level trust score remains separately not_reported.

No calibration acceptance criterion, numerical tolerance, observed coverage/reliability result or uncertainty estimate is reported. The unspecified threshold for clinician referral is a proposed routing threshold, not evidence that a calibration tolerance was achieved. Neither success nor failure can be assigned.

The paper motivates monitoring drift and responding to distribution shifts, and its abstract claims monitoring implementation. However, the supplied full text does not specify a shift statistic, reference distribution, detection threshold, shift-specific response or detection-performance experiment. Generic input screening and low-trust escalation do not sufficiently define an operational OOD detector.

No nonconformity score, conformal calibration split, coverage/error-control construction or exchangeability assumptions are reported for the trust framework. The illustrative weighted sum and unspecified escalation threshold do not establish conformal calibration; silence does not prove explicit non-use.

The paper claims safety and operational benefits from adaptive trust governance, so causal assessment of those benefits is relevant rather than automatically inapplicable. It does not define a population, comparison intervention, measured outcome, horizon and causal contrast for such an effect. Clinician referral is a proposed workflow operation, not a declared causal estimand.

For the asserted safety and efficiency benefits, the supplied full text provides no estimand-linked identification argument, allocation design, adjustment strategy or observed-data structure. The narrative applications and pipeline arrows do not identify an effect of adding trust scoring or clinician escalation. This is missing causal evidence, not a demonstrated failed identification procedure.

No consistency, exchangeability, positivity, interference, censoring or mechanistic identification assumptions are explicitly tied to an estimand for the framework's claimed benefits. The warning that models may agree for the wrong reasons concerns reliability of agreement, not a stated causal identification assumption. No assumptions are inferred from regulatory discussion or cited studies.

The paper asserts that trust scoring reduces errors, but the supplied eight-page text reports no sensitivity analysis addressing confounding, selection, censoring, intervention assumptions or support. Discussion of changing regulations and configurable weights is not causal sensitivity assessment.

The narrative applications do not define action-effect predictions or compare them with simulated potential outcomes, controlled interventions or a qualified causal benchmark. Claimed case-study benefits and cited trust studies do not establish this framework's counterfactual validation.

assertions.applicability_reason: The scoped contribution processes symptom queries and language-model responses through trust scoring and referral. It does not specify physical or pharmacological intervention-to-state dynamics, so mechanistic intervention semantics are outside this response-governance specification.
assertions.rationale: The scoring pseudocode is not a physiological mechanism. Clinical subject matter and references to patient history do not convert response arbitration into a mechanistic patient simulator.

Claims that trust monitoring reduces errors or protects patients are not accompanied by a defined effect estimand, identification argument, assumptions, support assessment, intervention-effect validation or sensitivity analysis. No justified causal-effect interpretation is established; this is not coded absent because the authors do not explicitly disclaim identification or report a contradictory causal test.

The proposed governance layer can forward or flag outputs, and the healthcare illustration describes clinician referral. An implemented blocking mechanism, operational definition of prohibited outputs and fail behavior are not reported. Listing 1 only computes a score and does not implement the proposed gate.

criteria_met: The healthcare workflow specifies a conditional clinician-referral route when a trust score falls below a threshold.
Decision governance distinguishes forwarding an output from flagging it for review.
criteria_missing: Operational score definitions and the threshold value or threshold-selection policy are not reported.
Whether the patient-facing recommendation is withheld pending review is not operationally specified.
An executed deferral mechanism and its behavior when review is unavailable are not established.
assertions.rationale: This assertion records only a partially specified deferral design. It does not establish that an implemented system can abstain or that deferral improves safety.

criteria_met: A below-threshold trust score is the proposed escalation trigger.
A human clinician is the designated review role.
criteria_missing: Availability and responsibility of the receiving clinician are not specified.
Required response, response time and fallback for failed or delayed handoff are not specified.
Operational routing and actual human participation are not demonstrated.
assertions.rationale: The trigger and receiving role are source-supported specification elements, but the complete operational escalation criterion is not met. A clinician box in the proposed workflow is not evidence of a human study or deployed handoff.

The abstract claims monitoring implementation, and the introduction proposes drift and consistency monitoring. The supplied methods do not establish an operational online detector connecting a defined failure signal to an implemented protective response. The illustrative scoring function has no monitoring cadence, drift rule, adaptive update or executed response path.

Clinician referral is proposed, but no tested stop, shutdown or safe-degradation mechanism is described. The paper does not specify what happens to pending outputs, ongoing processing or previously delivered advice after stopping or referral. The software-only setting does not itself make safe fallback inapplicable.

Input screening mentions adversarial patterns, biased phrasing and incomplete context. It does not provide an explicit asset inventory, adversary capabilities or attack-path analysis across the proposed system's interfaces. These generic screening concerns are insufficient for a documented threat model; no world-model attack analysis is inherited from citations.

No defined adversarial queries or injected faults, test population, attack protocol, safety-output measurements or results are reported for this framework. Recommending adversarial input screening does not establish an adversarial evaluation, and the lack of reported testing is not coded as an explicit negative experiment.

The healthcare illustration includes patient-history information, and the paper names GDPR and HIPAA in its regulatory discussion. It does not operationally specify de-identification, data minimization, access controls, encryption, differential privacy or a federated execution mechanism for this framework. Regulatory mentions and federated-learning bibliography entries do not establish implemented privacy controls.

Across the supplied text, no copying, membership-inference, re-identification or attribute-disclosure assessment of LLM responses or representations is reported. No audit threat model, attack procedure, disclosure metric or result is supplied. The conceptual status of the proposal does not demonstrate that such risks are absent or inapplicable.

The framework discusses patient-facing responses, patient-history inputs and clinician referral, but specifies no enforced identities, access permissions or authorized external-operation scopes. No EHR write, device actuation or external-system authorization is demonstrated. Human oversight and compliance scoring are not permission enforcement.
